title: Entity resolution & master data
blurb: Deciding which records refer to the same person, place or thing, and keeping one trusted version: what it takes, and which trade-offs are yours to own.

cards.prompt: Fellegi-Sunter: define the m- and u-probabilities for a field.
cards.answer: m = P(field agrees | the records are a true match). u = P(field agrees | the records are not a match).
cards.retiredWhy: Marked too detailed. Replaced by the leader-level rewrite you accepted.

cards.prompt: How do m and u become a match weight, and how do the weights combine?
cards.answer: Agreement on a field adds log2(m/u). Disagreement adds log2((1-m)/(1-u)). Assuming conditional independence, the field weights and the prior log-odds sum to a total match weight in log2 odds. Convert to a probability with p = 2^w / (1 + 2^w).
points: Agreement weight log2(m/u)
Disagreement weight log2((1-m)/(1-u))
Sum across fields plus prior (conditional independence)
Weight is log-odds; convert to probability
cards.retiredWhy: Marked too detailed: the weight arithmetic is implementation, not principle.

cards.prompt: What does blocking do, and what is its main failure mode?
cards.answer: Blocking compares only the record pairs that share a blocking key (say, same postcode and first initial), which turns n-squared comparisons into something tractable. Its failure mode is that a true match with an error in the blocking field is never compared at all. The fix is several blocking rules whose results are unioned.
points: Restricts comparisons to candidate pairs
Errors in the blocking field cause unrecoverable misses
Use several blocking rules, unioned
cards.retiredWhy: Implementation detail, below the level marked just right.

cards.prompt: Why should agreement on 'Zbigniewski' count for more than agreement on 'Smith'?
cards.answer: Because u depends on the value. Two random people are far more likely to share a common surname than a rare one. A term-frequency adjustment computes u from the frequency of that specific value, so agreement on a rare value counts as stronger evidence.
points: u varies by value frequency
Rare-value agreement is stronger evidence
Term-frequency adjustment
cards.retiredWhy: Implementation detail, below the level marked just right.

cards.prompt: How are u-probabilities usually estimated, and why does that work?
cards.answer: By randomly sampling record pairs. Almost all random pairs are non-matches, so their agreement rate approximates u. m comes from EM within blocks or from labeled pairs.
cards.retiredWhy: Implementation detail, below the level marked just right.

cards.prompt: You are linking people between two organizations' client datasets to coordinate services. How do you set match thresholds?
cards.answer: Use two thresholds: auto-link above the upper one, reject below the lower one, and send the band between them to clerical review. Set them from what each error costs in this use. A false merge, which combines two people's histories, usually does more harm in service settings (wrong eligibility, privacy exposure) than a missed link. Estimate precision and recall on a labeled sample, size the review band to the staff who will work it, and monitor for drift.
points: Two thresholds with a clerical-review band
Set from the asymmetric costs of false merges vs missed links
False merges usually worse in service contexts
Precision/recall on a labeled sample
Size the review band to capacity; monitor drift

cards.prompt: Why is an address string, on its own, a weak key for linking people?
cards.answer: Formats vary (St vs Street, unit designators, directionals). Many people share one address: households, multi-unit buildings, shelters. People move, so an address is only true for a period of time. PO boxes and institutional addresses add noise. Linking on address alone merges households into individuals.
points: Format variation
Shared addresses (households, multi-unit, shelters)
Temporal: people move
Conflates households with individuals

cards.prompt: A new matching method raises the match rate from 82% to 95%. Why isn't that evidence it's better?
cards.answer: Match rate counts how many records got a match, not whether the matches are right. Loosening any matcher raises the rate by adding false matches. Judge it by precision and recall against a labeled sample, and report both alongside the rate.
points: Match rate is not match accuracy
Looser matching inflates the rate with false matches
Measure precision and recall on labeled pairs
Report both, not the rate alone

cards.prompt: What is entity resolution, and why should a data leader care about it?
cards.answer: Entity resolution, also called record linkage or matching, decides which records within or across systems refer to the same real-world person, organization, place or thing when they share no reliable identifier. Without it the same entity is counted several times, its history is split across systems, and nobody can produce a single view of a customer or client. It brings two errors to govern: false merges, which combine different entities, and missed matches.
points: Decides which records refer to the same real-world entity
Needed when there is no shared, reliable identifier
Without it: double counting, split history, no single view
Two errors to govern: false merges and missed matches
cards.why: Why it matters: how many wrong merges and missed matches are acceptable is a business decision with real consequences, so it shouldn't be left as a technical default.

cards.prompt: Deterministic vs probabilistic matching: how does each decide, and what does each trade away?
cards.answer: Deterministic matching links records when chosen fields agree exactly, or by fixed rules. It's simple, fast and easy to explain, but it misses true matches that contain typos, name changes or missing values. Probabilistic matching weighs the evidence from several fields and scores how likely a pair is to be a match. It finds more true matches in messy data, but it needs thresholds, tuning and a review process for the uncertain cases.
points: Deterministic: exact agreement or fixed rules
Simple and explainable, but misses messy true matches
Probabilistic: weighs evidence across fields into a score
Finds more matches, but needs thresholds, tuning and review

cards.prompt: In master data management, what is a golden record, and what are survivorship rules?
cards.answer: A golden record is the single best version of an entity, assembled from the matched records in different systems. Survivorship rules decide which source's value wins for each attribute when the sources disagree: for example the most recently updated address, or the most trusted system for a date of birth. The rules encode judgments about which source to trust for what, so the business should own them and they should be written down.
points: Golden record: the best single version, built from matched records
Survivorship rules: which value wins, attribute by attribute
Typical rules: most recent, most trusted source, most complete
The rules are business decisions: owned and documented
cards.source: DAMA-DMBOK2, ch. 10 (Reference and Master Data); Loshin, Master Data Management (2009)

cards.prompt: Master data, reference data, transactional data: what is each?
cards.answer: Master data: the core entities the organization operates on, such as customers, products, employees and locations. Reference data: the code lists and classifications used to categorize other data, such as country or status codes. Transactional data: records of events involving those entities, such as orders and payments.
cards.why: Why it matters: master and reference data are shared across systems, so an error there spreads everywhere. That's why they get governed first.
